interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
A 1 m length of cable, 1000 mm, drawn as a bar with 0 at its left end and 1000 mm at its right, cut into four pieces by three cuts. The first piece, at the 0 end, is the one you set with the slider: its length in millimetres is written on it, and a label above it gives its name. The other three pieces share what is left of the metre equally, the picture's own choice so that one slider moves everything. Under the bar sits the test row: four copies of your first piece laid end to end from 0, against the same 0 to 1000 mm scale. That row is the claim the 4 on the bottom of 1/4 makes, drawn out.

The rule: a piece is a quarter of the metre when four pieces of its size make the metre, so 'Pieces this size in a metre' is 1000 ÷ the first piece's length, and the label follows that count: '1/4 of the metre' at 4, '1/5 of the metre' at 5, '1/10 of the metre' at 10, and 'not one piece of any equal cut' when the count is not a whole number, because then no equal cut of the metre has this piece as one of its pieces. At the opening setting, 250 mm, 1000 ÷ 250 = 4: the four copies end exactly on the 1000 mm mark, the other three pieces are (1000 − 250) ÷ 3 = 250 mm each, all four match, and the label reads 1/4 of the metre. Slide to 200 mm and 1000 ÷ 200 = 5: five pieces of that size make the metre, so the copies stop at 4 × 200 = 800 mm, short of the end, and the label reads 1/5 of the metre although the piece is still one of four on the bar. The other three are then (1000 − 200) ÷ 3, about 266.67 mm each, shown rounded as 267, and 'Pieces their size in a metre' is 3.75, not a whole number, so they are not quarters either. At 100 mm ten fit and the label reads 1/10 of the metre; the other three are 300 mm each, about 3.33 to the metre. At 400 mm only 2.5 fit, so the copies run on to 1600 mm and are cut off at the drawing's edge, while the other three are 200 mm each, which do fit five times: honest fifths, though the first piece is not one piece of any equal cut.

As equations, with L the first piece's length in millimetres: pieces this size in a metre = 1000 ÷ L; each of the other three = (1000 − L) ÷ 3; pieces their size in a metre = 1000 ÷ ((1000 − L) ÷ 3), which comes to 3000 ÷ (1000 − L), so at 200 mm it is 3000 ÷ 800 = 3.75. The two counting readouts show two decimal places, so an honest count reads as a whole number, 4.00 or 5.00 or 10.00, and a piece that is not one piece of any equal cut shows something after the point.
interactive.ignores: The other three pieces always come out equal to one another, which could suggest that is how cable gets cut; it is only the picture's way of letting one slider move everything, and a real metre can be cut into four pieces of four different lengths. The test row copies your piece four times; on the job you would lay the one piece against the whole with a tape, or measure both, rather than cut copies. The lengths are shown as exact millimetres and the copies as meeting edge to edge; a real cut loses a little to the blade and is never that exact. Only length is shown: pieces of a board's area or of a set of parts follow the same rule, equal amounts of the whole, but look different. A readout such as 3.33 or 2.5 is how many pieces fit, not a fraction's name, and the label 'not one piece of any equal cut' does not mean the piece has no name: a 300 mm piece is three of the 100 mm pieces, and 100 mm fits ten times, so by the last lesson's counting it is 3/10 of the metre; its fit count is not a whole number because three tenths do not go evenly into the ten that make the metre, so it is not one piece of any equal cut.

explain.text:
Four pieces are not four quarters; four equal pieces are. The 4 on the bottom of 1/4 does not simply count how many bits a thing has been cut into. It is a claim about size: that four pieces of this size, laid end to end, make exactly one whole. Remember from the last lesson that the bottom number names the piece and the top counts the pieces? That only works because every piece is the same size, and this lesson is about what happens when they are not: the names stop being true.

Start with why equal matters, from the counting you already trust. A fraction's whole is always divided into equal pieces,[^1] and the bottom number says how many equal pieces there are in total,[^2] which is the same as saying how many of them make up one whole.[^3] The top number counts how many of those pieces you have.[^4] Now that you know what each one does, here are their textbook names: the bottom number is the [[denominator]] and the top number is the [[numerator]]. This course goes on calling them the bottom and top number, but when you meet the long names you will know what each is counting. Both numbers are talking about one size of piece, so between them they fix one length: the size of the piece from the bottom, the count from the top. Cut the pieces unequal and that link snaps. The bottom number no longer tells you the size of any piece, because there is no one size, and the top number no longer tells you how much you have, because three big pieces and three small ones both count as three. Writing 1/4 on one of those unequal pieces because it is one of four would be a false label unless the piece happens to be the right size: it is some fraction of the whole, just not necessarily that one. **A piece is a quarter when four pieces of its size make the whole, and the way to check is to ask how many of it fit: the whole divided by the piece.**

Now the worked example, with real cable. Take a 1 m length, 1000 mm, and cut it into four equal pieces. Each is 1000 ÷ 4 = 250 mm, and four laid end to end give 4 × 250 = 1000 mm, the whole metre back. Each piece passes the test, 1000 ÷ 250 = 4, so each is honestly a quarter, 1/4 of the metre, and any two of them are 2/4 of it, which is 500 mm, half the metre. Now cut a second metre into four unequal pieces instead: 100 mm, then three of 300 mm. Still four pieces. Is the 100 mm piece a quarter? Run the test: 1000 ÷ 100 = 10, so ten of them make the metre and the piece is a tenth, 1/10 of the metre, even though it was one of four. Four of it laid end to end reach only 400 mm. The 300 mm pieces are not quarters either: 1000 ÷ 300 is about 3.33, not a whole number, so no equal cut of the metre has a 300 mm piece as one of its pieces, and four of them would be 1200 mm, past the end of the metre. It still has an honest name, found by the counting from the last lesson: it is three of the 100 mm pieces, and ten of those make the metre, so it is three tenths, 3/10 of the metre. In the picture the slider runs this test for you. At 250 mm the four copies under the bar end exactly on the 1000 mm mark and the label reads 1/4 of the metre; move the first piece to 200 mm and the copies stop at 800 mm, the readout shows that five pieces of that size fit the metre, and the label changes to 1/5 of the metre, while the bar above still shows four pieces. Notice that a 250 mm piece is a quarter of the metre however the rest of the metre was cut, because the test is about the piece and the whole alone; what the four-piece bar shows is that cutting into four does not, by itself, make any of the pieces a quarter.

Here is the habit to watch, failing. Suppose someone cuts the metre 100, 300, 300, 300, hands you two of the four pieces and says 'that's half a metre: two quarters'. Two quarters of 1000 mm would be 500 mm. What you are holding is 100 + 300 = 400 mm, or 300 + 300 = 600 mm, depending on which two you were given. Neither is half, and an answer that changes with the pick is exactly what a fraction is supposed to rule out. People who study how fractions are learned list treating the top and bottom as two independent whole numbers among the common errors.[^5] The four-pieces habit is a cousin of that error: it reads the bottom as a plain count of bits rather than as the claim that four equal pieces make the whole.

One last thing about the word equal: it means the same amount of the whole, not the same look. A whole can be divided into any number of equal pieces,[^6] four or five or ten, and equal pieces do not need to look the same.[^7] A square of board cut into four strips and the same square cut into a two-by-two grid both give quarters: the strips and the small squares are different shapes but the same amount of board, and four of either make the whole square. Cable has only length to share, so for cable equal just means the same length.

**The bottom number is a claim about size, not a tally of pieces: a piece is a quarter only when four of its size make the whole, so before you read the number of pieces as the bottom number, check that they are equal.[^1][^3]**

analogy.text: You already know this from a three-phase board. Three phases do not make each phase a third of the load; three equal loads do. Say a board is carrying 30 kW with 10 kW on each phase: 30 ÷ 10 = 3, so three of that size make the whole and each phase carries an honest third, 1/3 of the load. Put 20 kW on one phase and 5 kW on each of the other two and the 20 kW phase is still one of three, but 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5, so it is not a third of the load. Three phases all along; the count never earned the name, only equal shares did.
analogy.breaks: A cut metre of cable stays cut; a board's whole, its total load, changes as people switch things on and off, so a phase's share drifts through the day while a fraction of a fixed whole stays put. And the pieces of a cable are all one kind of thing laid end to end, whereas the three phase currents are out of step with one another in time, so currents do not add across phases the way lengths do. That is why the comparison is made in kilowatts, which do add plainly across the phases, and not in amps.

practice.text:
Checking any fraction's name before you trust it:
- Ask what the whole is: the metre, the drum, the board's total load, the full length on the drawing.
- Ask whether the pieces are equal in amount (length, area, load), not whether there are the right number of them.
- Test the piece's name by the fit: whole ÷ piece. A whole-number answer is the piece's bottom number with 1 on top (fits five times: 1/5); a quarter fits four times, a fifth five, a tenth ten.
- If the pieces are not equal, do not read the piece count as a bottom number. Measure the piece against the whole and name it from the fit instead.

**Rules of thumb:** the bottom number (the denominator) is how many pieces of one size make the whole, and the number of pieces you can see agrees with it only when they are all equal; the top number (the numerator) counts how many pieces of that one size you have. Equal means the same amount, not the same look. A fit count that is not a whole number means the piece is not a single piece of any equal cut of that whole, so name it by counting pieces of a size that does fit: a 300 mm piece is three of the 100 mm pieces, and 100 mm fits the metre ten times, so it is 3/10 of the metre.

**Worked example:** say a 50 m drum of cable is cut into four runs, 20 m, 10 m, 10 m and 10 m, and someone calls each run a quarter of the drum. A quarter of 50 m is 50 ÷ 4 = 12.5 m, and no run is that long. Test a 10 m run: 50 ÷ 10 = 5, so five of them make the drum and each 10 m run is a fifth, 1/5 of the drum. Test the 20 m run: 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5, not a whole number, so no equal cut of the drum has it as a single piece, and four of it would be 80 m, more than the drum holds; it is two of the 10 m runs, so it is two fifths, 2/5 of the drum. Four runs, no quarters.

**Common mistakes:**
- Reading the bottom number as 'how many pieces I can see'. Four pieces are quarters only when all four match; count the fit, not the pieces.
- Judging equal by eye. Pieces of different shapes can be equal amounts of the whole,[^7] and pieces that look alike need not be: measure.
- Losing track of the whole, as in the last lesson: a quarter of a 1 m tail and a quarter of a 50 m drum are different lengths, and comparing two fractions is only valid when both refer to the same whole,[^8] so test each piece against its own whole.
- Expecting real cuts to be perfect. Every cut loses a little to the blade and to your eye, so a real quarter is honest to the precision you can measure, which is usually all a job needs; when the job depends on it, measure each piece against the whole rather than trusting the count.

A 1 m length of cable, 1000 mm, cut into four pieces: the first piece is set by the slider, the other three share the rest equally, and under the bar four copies of the first piece lie end to end from 0.

A piece is a quarter when four of its size make the metre: the whole divided by the piece says how many fit.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the four copies under the bar miss the 1000 mm mark and the label stop saying 1/4, while the bar still shows four pieces, when you slide the first piece off 250 mm.

checks.label: At 250 mm, 1000 ÷ 250 = 4 pieces fit, the copies end at 1000 mm, the other three are 250 mm and fit 4 times: 1/4 of the metre
At 200 mm, 5 pieces fit and the copies stop at 800 mm, short of the metre; the other three are 267 mm and 3.75 of them fit: 1/5 of the metre
At 100 mm, 10 pieces fit (1/10 of the metre) and the copies reach only 400 mm; the other three are 300 mm, four of which would be 1200 mm, past the end, and 3.33 fit
At 400 mm only 2.5 pieces fit, so the copies run on to 1600 mm and the piece is not one piece of any equal cut; the other three are 200 mm, honest fifths

The bottom number says how many pieces of this size make up the whole: the label reads one over that count exactly when a whole number of pieces of the first piece's size make the metre, and the four pieces on the bar always add up to the whole metre

applied.problem: 'Writing 1/4 on one of those unequal pieces would be a false label' is too general: a piece in an unequal four-way cut can still be an honest quarter (a 250 mm piece, as the lesson itself says two paragraphs later, or the 200 mm fifths at the slider's 400 mm end).

The rule of thumb says the bottom number is how many of 'this piece' make the whole, which is false for the 3/10 piece named in the same paragraph (ten 300 mm pieces do not make a metre); the bottom counts pieces of the one size, which the top then counts.

'not a whole number because the piece is several tenths' states a false reason: five tenths are several tenths yet fit the metre exactly twice; the fit is not whole because three tenths do not go evenly into the ten that make the whole.
